articleData.summary: An evidence-linked learning object for years 1–3. It contains 14 atomic concepts and preserves exact source locators; unsupported template sections remain explicitly empty.
articleData.body:
### Orientation

Evidence not yet available for this section; no content was inferred.

### Components and relations

The heart is covered by fibrous and serous pericardial sacs.

The heart lies within the pericardium in the middle mediastinum.

The mediastinal surfaces of the left pleura and lung relate to the left anterior aspect of the aortic arch.

The heart lies behind the sternum and costal cartilages.

Spiral aorticopulmonary septum explains pulmonary trunk passing anterior, left, then posterior to ascending aorta.

Contents of the anterior mediastinum are anterior relations of the sternocostal surface.

Superior and inferior sternopericardial ligaments attach the pericardium to the sternum.

From superior to inferior, the descending thoracic aorta relates anteriorly to left principal bronchus, pericardium, esophagus, and diaphragm.

The anterior septal border corresponds to the anterior interventricular groove on the sternocostal surface.

The sternocostal surface is related anteriorly to the sternum and second through sixth costal cartilages.

The upper border is formed mainly by the left atrium and to a lesser extent by the right atrium.

A tricuspid cusp base attaches to the fibrous ring, while its free border attaches to chordae tendineae.

A papillary muscle base attaches to the ventricular wall and its apex gives rise to chordae tendineae.

Valve sounds are best heard at auscultatory areas rather than directly over anatomical valve positions because sound propagates.

articleData.summary: An evidence-linked learning object for years 1–3. It contains 14 atomic concepts and preserves exact source locators; unsupported template sections remain explicitly empty.
articleData.body:
### Orientation

Evidence not yet available for this section; no content was inferred.

### Components and relations

The heart has two atria and two ventricles.

The moderator band prevents overdistension of the right ventricle.

The atrioventricular bundle arises from the A-V node and traverses the fibrous skeleton to reach the interventricular septum.

The entire interventricular septum may be absent.

The aortic valve projects as a 2.5-cm oblique line behind the left sternal margin opposite the third left intercostal space.

The mitral valve projects as a 3-cm oblique line behind the left half of the sternum opposite the fourth left sternocostal junction.

The pulmonary valve projects as a 2.5-cm horizontal line behind the third left costal cartilage at the sternum.

The tricuspid valve projects as a 4-cm vertical line behind the center of the sternum opposite the fourth intercostal space.

Chordae from the anterior papillary muscle attach to the anterior and posterior tricuspid cusps.

The anterior papillary muscle is the largest right ventricular papillary muscle.

In TGA, aorta connects to right ventricle.

The aortic orifice is circular, lies horizontally at the upper aortic vestibule, and is surrounded by a fibrous ring attaching the three aortic cusps.

Three slight dilatations of the ascending aortic root opposite the cusps are called aortic sinuses.

At its beginning, the ascending aorta has three aortic sinuses opposite the aortic-valve cusps: one anterior and two posterior.

articleData.summary: An evidence-linked learning object for years 1–3. It contains 14 atomic concepts and preserves exact source locators; unsupported template sections remain explicitly empty.
articleData.body:
### Orientation

Evidence not yet available for this section; no content was inferred.

### Components and relations

A balanced pattern has two posterior interventricular branches, one from each coronary artery.

The small cardiac vein turns backward-left in the coronary sulcus with the right coronary artery.

The right marginal artery supplies the right ventricle.

The posterior interventricular artery gives an A-V node and bundle artery in 80% of people.

Two to four anterior cardiac veins arise from the anterior wall of the right ventricle and penetrate the anterior right atrial wall.

The ascending aorta gives the right and left coronary arteries as its two branches.

Most cardiac veins accompany arteries.

The circumflex artery accompanies the coronary sinus, with blood flowing in the same direction in both vessels.

Blockage of a coronary artery or major branch can cause myocardial infarction, defined here as death of myocardium.

Narrowing of a large coronary branch can reduce cardiac blood supply and cause myocardial ischemia.

The coronary sinus opens between the inferior vena cava and tricuspid orifices and is guarded by a rudimentary valve.

The coronary sinus runs left to right with the circumflex artery.

The anterior interventricular artery descends with the great cardiac vein to the inferior border 1.5 cm right of the apex.

The circumflex artery travels through anterior and posterior coronary sulcus and ends by anastomosing with the right coronary artery.

sections.heading: Components and relations
sections.body:
A balanced pattern has two posterior interventricular branches, one from each coronary artery.

The small cardiac vein turns backward-left in the coronary sulcus with the right coronary artery.

The right marginal artery supplies the right ventricle.

The posterior interventricular artery gives an A-V node and bundle artery in 80% of people.

Two to four anterior cardiac veins arise from the anterior wall of the right ventricle and penetrate the anterior right atrial wall.

The ascending aorta gives the right and left coronary arteries as its two branches.

Most cardiac veins accompany arteries.

The circumflex artery accompanies the coronary sinus, with blood flowing in the same direction in both vessels.

Blockage of a coronary artery or major branch can cause myocardial infarction, defined here as death of myocardium.

Narrowing of a large coronary branch can reduce cardiac blood supply and cause myocardial ischemia.

The coronary sinus opens between the inferior vena cava and tricuspid orifices and is guarded by a rudimentary valve.

The coronary sinus runs left to right with the circumflex artery.

The anterior interventricular artery descends with the great cardiac vein to the inferior border 1.5 cm right of the apex.

The circumflex artery travels through anterior and posterior coronary sulcus and ends by anastomosing with the right coronary artery.

### Core definition

A cardiac murmur is an abnormal heart sound heard over chest-wall auscultatory areas

Abnormal heart sounds may have altered intensity

About 80% of resting ventricular filling occurs before atrial contraction

All valves are closed and ventricular volume is constant during isovolumetric relaxation

Aortic and pulmonary pressures fall during atrial systole as blood runs to the periphery

At resting heart rate 75/min, one cardiac cycle lasts about 0.8 s

Atrial contribution to ventricular filling increases during exercise

Atrial diastole lasts about 0.7 s

Atrial systole lasts about 0.1 s

Atrial systole overlaps the final 0.1 s of ventricular diastole and is termed late diastole

Atrial systole raises ventricular pressure to about 9 mmHg left and 4 mmHg right

Atrial-to-ventricular flow during atrial systole produces the fourth heart sound

articleData.body:
### What the test measures

P waves are absent in atrial fibrillation

A +30° depolarization vector produces equal positive waves in leads I and II

A 12-lead ECG uses ten electrodes: one on each limb and six on the chest

A depolarization vector aligned with a lead's positive axis produces that lead's maximal positive wave

A fibrous tissue disc electrically separates atrial and ventricular myocytes

A premature beat is an extra beat caused by a premature cardiac electrical impulse

A Q wave is considered abnormal when its height exceeds 25% of the R wave in the same QRS complex

A sufficiently large delayed afterdepolarization activates sodium current and triggers activity

A sufficiently large early afterdepolarization can trigger an action potential

Action potentials spread between ventricular myocytes at about 0.5 m/s

Action potentials spread through atrial myocytes at about 0.5 m/s

Afterdepolarizations are depolarizations triggered by preceding action potentials

An electrically silent infarct acts as an electric hole exposing vectors from the opposite heart wall

An electrocardiogram is the tracing of cardiac currents recorded by body-surface electrodes

### Core definition

A large artery 105 cm below the heart is calculated near 180 mmHg

A large artery 50 cm above the heart is calculated near 62 mmHg

About 24 L fluid are filtered through capillaries daily

About 64% of blood volume is in systemic veins

About 7% of blood volume is in arterioles and capillaries

About 85% of filtered capillary fluid is reabsorbed at venous ends

Above the right atrium, venous pressure falls 0.77 mmHg/cm and neck veins may collapse below atmospheric pressure

Absence of valves between right atrium and venae cavae transmits right-atrial pressure waves to jugular veins

Active-tissue metabolites recruit more capillaries and accelerate vasomotion

After hemorrhage, reduced capillary hydrostatic pressure draws interstitial fluid into capillaries and expands plasma volume

All cardiac capillaries are described as open, without vasomotion

Angiotensin II directly constricts arterioles and veins

articleSpans.text: The heart is covered by fibrous and serous pericardial sacs.
The heart lies within the pericardium in the middle mediastinum.
The mediastinal surfaces of the left pleura and lung relate to the left anterior aspect of the aortic arch.
The heart lies behind the sternum and costal cartilages.
Spiral aorticopulmonary septum explains pulmonary trunk passing anterior, left, then posterior to ascending aorta.
Contents of the anterior mediastinum are anterior relations of the sternocostal surface.
Superior and inferior sternopericardial ligaments attach the pericardium to the sternum.
From superior to inferior, the descending thoracic aorta relates anteriorly to left principal bronchus, pericardium, esophagus, and diaphragm.
The anterior septal border corresponds to the anterior interventricular groove on the sternocostal surface.
The sternocostal surface is related anteriorly to the sternum and second through sixth costal cartilages.
The upper border is formed mainly by the left atrium and to a lesser extent by the right atrium.
A tricuspid cusp base attaches to the fibrous ring, while its free border attaches to chordae tendineae.
A papillary muscle base attaches to the ventricular wall and its apex gives rise to chordae tendineae.
Valve sounds are best heard at auscultatory areas rather than directly over anatomical valve positions because sound propagates.
The heart has two atria and two ventricles.
The moderator band prevents overdistension of the right ventricle.
The atrioventricular bundle arises from the A-V node and traverses the fibrous skeleton to reach the interventricular septum.
The entire interventricular septum may be absent.
The aortic valve projects as a 2.5-cm oblique line behind the left sternal margin opposite the third left intercostal space.
The mitral valve projects as a 3-cm oblique line behind the left half of the sternum opposite the fourth left sternocostal junction.
The pulmonary valve projects as a 2.5-cm horizontal line behind the third left costal cartilage at the sternum.
The tricuspid valve projects as a 4-cm vertical line behind the center of the sternum opposite the fourth intercostal space.
Chordae from the anterior papillary muscle attach to the anterior and posterior tricuspid cusps.
The anterior papillary muscle is the largest right ventricular papillary muscle.
In TGA, aorta connects to right ventricle.
The aortic orifice is circular, lies horizontally at the upper aortic vestibule, and is surrounded by a fibrous ring attaching the three aortic cusps.
Three slight dilatations of the ascending aortic root opposite the cusps are called aortic sinuses.
At its beginning, the ascending aorta has three aortic sinuses opposite the aortic-valve cusps: one anterior and two posterior.
A balanced pattern has two posterior interventricular branches, one from each coronary artery.
The small cardiac vein turns backward-left in the coronary sulcus with the right coronary artery.
The right marginal artery supplies the right ventricle.
The posterior interventricular artery gives an A-V node and bundle artery in 80% of people.
Two to four anterior cardiac veins arise from the anterior wall of the right ventricle and penetrate the anterior right atrial wall.
The ascending aorta gives the right and left coronary arteries as its two branches.
Most cardiac veins accompany arteries.
The circumflex artery accompanies the coronary sinus, with blood flowing in the same direction in both vessels.
Blockage of a coronary artery or major branch can cause myocardial infarction, defined here as death of myocardium.
Narrowing of a large coronary branch can reduce cardiac blood supply and cause myocardial ischemia.
The coronary sinus opens between the inferior vena cava and tricuspid orifices and is guarded by a rudimentary valve.
The coronary sinus runs left to right with the circumflex artery.
The anterior interventricular artery descends with the great cardiac vein to the inferior border 1.5 cm right of the apex.
The circumflex artery travels through anterior and posterior coronary sulcus and ends by anastomosing with the right coronary artery.
A non-pacemaker cardiac myocyte is rapidly depolarized from about −90 mV resting potential to a −65 mV firing level
Acetylcholine binding muscarinic receptors lowers cAMP and funny current in sinoatrial cells
Adjacent active myocytes trigger non-pacemaker action potentials by cell-to-cell depolarizing current
Adrenal epinephrine and norepinephrine increase sinoatrial firing by mechanisms resembling sympathetic stimulation
Atrial flutter is usually regular though conduction block may change
Atrioventricular block disturbs conduction between atria and ventricles
Atrioventricular block may prolong PR or produce P waves not followed by QRS
Atrioventricular delay lets atria complete contraction and empty into ventricles before ventricular contraction
Atrioventricular-node conduction delays atrial-to-ventricular impulse arrival by about 0.1 second
Automaticity and rhythmicity arise from spontaneous regular pacemaker action potentials
AV block can increase PR interval or produce P waves without following QRS complexes
AV block is disturbed conduction between atria and ventricles at the atrioventricular node
Block of the premature impulse in pathway A with conduction through pathway B constitutes unidirectional block
Body fluids conduct cardiac potential changes to the skin surface
Endocardium has an inner endothelial layer
A prominent internal elastic lamina distinguishes muscular from elastic arteries
Aorta and its large branches are large elastic arteries
Arterioles regulate blood flow to capillaries
Arteriovenous anastomoses directly connect arterioles and venules without capillary passage
Continuous capillaries occur in connective tissue, bone, skin, and exocrine glands
Fenestrated capillaries occur in intestine, endocrine glands, and renal glomeruli
Many muscular arteries have a recognizable external elastic lamina
Material exchange between blood and tissues occurs through capillaries and postcapillary venules
Medium muscular arteries include most muscular and organ arteries
Pericyte contraction regulates capillary blood flow
Pericyte processes usually surround capillary endothelium
Postcapillary venule media contains pericytes and reticular fibers
Renal glomerular capillary fenestrae lack diaphragms
A cardiac murmur is an abnormal heart sound heard over chest-wall auscultatory areas
Abnormal heart sounds may have altered intensity
About 80% of resting ventricular filling occurs before atrial contraction
All valves are closed and ventricular volume is constant during isovolumetric relaxation
Aortic and pulmonary pressures fall during atrial systole as blood runs to the periphery
Arterial pressure reaches about 80 mmHg aortic and 10 mmHg pulmonary during isovolumetric contraction
At resting heart rate 75/min, one cardiac cycle lasts about 0.8 s
Atrial contraction contributes about 20% of resting ventricular filling
Atrial contribution to ventricular filling increases during exercise
Atrial diastole lasts about 0.7 s
Atrial systole lasts about 0.1 s
Atrial systole overlaps the final 0.1 s of ventricular diastole and is termed late diastole
Atrial systole raises ventricular pressure to about 9 mmHg left and 4 mmHg right
Atrial-to-ventricular flow during atrial systole produces the fourth heart sound
A low ejection fraction indicates heart failure
A weak myocardium initially cannot pump excess venous return, causing right-atrial blood accumulation and pressure elevation
Active tension required to move the load measures afterload
Adenosine inhibits cAMP production and reduces cardiac contractility
After blood-volume expansion, stress relaxation limits increases in mean systemic filling pressure, venous return, cardiac output, and arterial pressure
After blood-volume loss, reverse stress relaxation limits falls in mean systemic filling pressure, venous return, cardiac output, and arterial pressure
After reaching afterload, the muscle shortens while supporting the load
Afterload is the load against which cardiac muscle contracts
Afterload mainly affects end-systolic volume
ANP lowers blood volume, central venous pressure, cardiac output, and arterial pressure
Anxiety and excitement can increase cardiac output
Arterial pressure equals cardiac output multiplied by total peripheral resistance
Arterial pressure equals heart rate multiplied by stroke volume and total peripheral resistance
As cardiac output falls, mean arterial pressure falls and right-atrial pressure rises from venous backup
P waves are absent in atrial fibrillation
A +30° depolarization vector produces equal positive waves in leads I and II
A 12-lead ECG uses ten electrodes: one on each limb and six on the chest
A depolarization vector aligned with a lead's positive axis produces that lead's maximal positive wave
A fibrous tissue disc electrically separates atrial and ventricular myocytes
A premature beat is an extra beat caused by a premature cardiac electrical impulse
A Q wave is considered abnormal when its height exceeds 25% of the R wave in the same QRS complex
A sufficiently large delayed afterdepolarization activates sodium current and triggers activity
A sufficiently large early afterdepolarization can trigger an action potential
Action potentials spread between ventricular myocytes at about 0.5 m/s
Action potentials spread through atrial myocytes at about 0.5 m/s
Afterdepolarizations are depolarizations triggered by preceding action potentials
An electrically silent infarct acts as an electric hole exposing vectors from the opposite heart wall
An electrocardiogram is the tracing of cardiac currents recorded by body-surface electrodes
A hand pump inflates or deflates the cuff through a one-way valve
Above systolic pressure the brachial artery is completely collapsed and silent
Acute emotional or threatening stimuli raise arterial pressure and heart rate, increase skeletal-muscle flow, and constrict splanchnic, renal, and cutaneous vessels
An appropriately sized cuff covers two-thirds of the biceps
An excessively loose cuff may cause falsely high blood pressure
An inelastic cuff transmits bag pressure uniformly to arm tissues and artery
Angiotensin II and reduced baroreceptor discharge stimulate thirst in hemorrhagic shock
Angiotensin II raises arterial pressure by increasing sympathetic activity during intermediate regulation
Angiotensin II raises arterial pressure through vasoconstriction during intermediate regulation
Aortic-arch baroreceptor afferents travel in the aortic nerve and vagus nerve
Arterial baroreceptors are located mainly in the carotid sinus and aortic arch
Arterial baroreceptors are mechanical stretch receptors that sense arterial pressure
Arterial baroreceptors begin responding near an arterial pressure of 50 mmHg
Arterial blood pressure is lateral pressure exerted by blood on the arterial wall
A large artery 105 cm below the heart is calculated near 180 mmHg
A large artery 50 cm above the heart is calculated near 62 mmHg
About 24 L fluid are filtered through capillaries daily
About 64% of blood volume is in systemic veins
About 7% of blood volume is in arterioles and capillaries
About 85% of filtered capillary fluid is reabsorbed at venous ends
Above the right atrium, venous pressure falls 0.77 mmHg/cm and neck veins may collapse below atmospheric pressure
Absence of valves between right atrium and venae cavae transmits right-atrial pressure waves to jugular veins
Active-tissue metabolites recruit more capillaries and accelerate vasomotion
Adding 200 mL to veins raises venous pressure by only about 1 mmHg, demonstrating high capacity
After 3–5 hours of refractory shock, precapillary sphincters dilate while venules remain constricted
After hemorrhage, reduced capillary hydrostatic pressure draws interstitial fluid into capillaries and expands plasma volume
All cardiac capillaries are described as open, without vasomotion
Angiotensin II directly constricts arterioles and veins
